title: How TESS works
summary: The satellite behind the light curves on this site: what it watches, for how long, and from where.

badge.name: Sector scout
badge.text: You know how TESS scans the sky one sector at a time.

steps.heading: A survey satellite
body: TESS, the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched in 2018. Its job is to watch about 200,000 nearby stars for the small, repeating dips in light that a passing planet causes.

facts.text: TESS was designed to monitor 200,000 nearby stars for planets.

steps.heading: One sector at a time
body: TESS stares at one long strip of sky, called a sector, measuring 24° by 96°. It watches each sector for about 27 days, then turns to the next.
Sectors overlap near the poles of the ecliptic, so stars there are watched for nearly a full year.

facts.text: Each sector measures 24° by 96° and is watched for about 27 days on average.

source.name: MIT TESS Science Office: TESS Observations

checks.quote: TESS observes the sky in sectors measuring 24° x 96°. Each sector is observed for two orbits of the satellite around the Earth, or about 27 days on average.

facts.text: A region centered on the ecliptic pole can be observed for nearly a full year.

source.name: MIT TESS Science Office: TESS Observations

checks.quote: centered on the ecliptic pole can be observed for nearly a full year

steps.heading: Its orbit
body: TESS goes around Earth on a long, stretched orbit, between 108,400 and 376,300 km from Earth, timed with the Moon: TESS goes around twice for every once of the Moon.

facts.text: TESS's orbit runs from 108,400 to 376,300 km and is in 2:1 resonance with the Moon.

checks.quote: 2:1 lunar resonance orbit of 108,400 by 376,300 kilometers

questions.prompt: About how many days does TESS watch each sector?
questions.explanation: Each sector is watched for two TESS orbits, about 27 days on average.
